title: Given K sorted integer lists, find the smallest range that includes at least one number from each of the K lists. If several ranges are equally small, return the one with the smaller start. Explain the K-way Merge technique and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists (Find the Tightest Range Including One Element from Each List)

s1_definition.profdef: Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists is a K-way Merge problem. We keep a min-heap of one current element per list and separately track the maximum of those current elements. The current window spans from the heap minimum to the tracked maximum and already covers every list. We repeatedly record the window, pop the minimum, and push its successor, updating the maximum; the smallest window ever seen is the answer. Time is N log K and space is K.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has K sorted lists of interest rates from K lenders. We want the narrowest rate band that still contains at least one rate from every lender. A clerk keeps the current lowest unused rate per lender, notes the highest of those, and the band from lowest to highest covers everyone. The clerk nudges the lowest rate forward, trying to shrink the band, and remembers the tightest band seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: The window from heap-min to running-max always covers all lists; shrink it by advancing the minimum.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists is a K-way Merge problem. We keep a min-heap of one current element per list and separately track the maximum of those current elements. The current window spans from the heap minimum to the tracked maximum and already covers every list. We repeatedly record the window, pop the minimum, and push its successor, updating the maximum; the smallest window ever seen is the answer. Time is N log K and space is K.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has K sorted lists of interest rates from K lenders. We want the narrowest rate band that still contains at least one rate from every lender. A clerk keeps the current lowest unused rate per lender, notes the highest of those, and the band from lowest to highest covers everyone. The clerk nudges the lowest rate forward, trying to shrink the band, and remembers the tightest band seen.

**One line to remember:** The window from heap-min to running-max always covers all lists; shrink it by advancing the minimum.

sections.s2_technical:
The crucial invariant is that if the heap holds exactly one element from each list, then the span from the smallest of them to the largest of them necessarily contains at least one element from every list. So that span is a valid covering range at all times.

We seed the heap with each list's first element and compute the maximum of those seeds. Each iteration: read the heap minimum, compare the span `max - min` against the best so far and update if tighter, then pop the minimum and push its successor while updating the running maximum with the pushed value. The moment any list runs out, no further window can cover all lists, so we stop.

In code the heap entry is `{value, listIndex, elementIndex}` ordered by value, and we hold a separate `int currentMax`. On each push we do `currentMax = Math.max(currentMax, nextValue)`. Senior nuance: the stop condition is reached exactly when the popped element has no successor, because advancing is the only way to keep all lists represented, and ties on window width are resolved by keeping the first (smaller-start) window since we only replace when strictly tighter.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India compares home-loan interest rates from K lenders, each lender's quotes stored sorted. The pricing team wants to advertise the tightest rate band that still includes at least one real quote from every lender, so the advertisement is honest for all of them. This is exactly how Smallest Number Range works: it finds the narrowest covering window.

The code defines a `RateBandService` exposing `smallestRange(lists)` returning a two-element array with the band start and end. A `Demo` builds three sorted rate lists (scaled to integers) and logs the tightest covering band.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is three sorted lists: lender one 4, 10, 15, 24; lender two 0, 9, 12, 20; lender three 5, 18, 22, 30.

Step 1 — We seed the heap with 4, 0, and 5. The running maximum is 5. The current band is from the minimum 0 to the maximum 5, width five, which covers all three lists.

Step 2 — We record band [0, 5]. We pop the minimum 0 from lender two and push its successor 9, which raises the maximum to 9. The band becomes [4, 9], width five. We record it, keeping the earlier equal-width band start rule so [0,5] stays best for now because [4,9] is not strictly tighter.

Step 3 — We pop 4 from lender one, push 10, maximum becomes 10. Band [5, 10], width five, not tighter.

Step 4 — We pop 5 from lender three, push 18, maximum becomes 18. Band [9, 18], width nine, not tighter. We continue popping and the windows widen.

Step 5 — Eventually a list runs out and we stop. The tightest band recorded was [0, 5], shown below as the smallest covering range.


```
  Input: 3 sorted rate lists
    L1: 4 10 15 24   L2: 0 9 12 20   L3: 5 18 22 30
    │
    ▼
  Seed heap {4,0,5}, max = 5, band = [0,5]  ← covers all
    │
    ▼
  Loop while every list represented:
    │ record band, pop min, push successor, update max
    │ [0,5] width 5  ← best
    │ [4,9] width 5
    │ [5,10] width 5
    │ [9,18] width 9 ...
    ▼ (one list exhausted → stop)
  Output: smallest covering band = [0, 5]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Smallest Number Range Covering K Lists is a K-way Merge problem built on one clean invariant. If my min-heap holds exactly one element from each list, then the span from the smallest of those elements to the largest of them must contain at least one number from every list, so that span is always a valid covering range. I keep the heap minimum and separately track the running maximum of whatever is currently in the heap.

To shrink the range I repeatedly record the current span, pop the minimum, and push its successor from the same list while updating the running maximum. Advancing the minimum is the only lever that can tighten the window, and the maximum can only stay or rise. The instant any list runs out, no further window can cover all lists, so I stop. Ties on width are resolved toward the smaller start because I only replace the best when a new window is strictly tighter.

At the National Bank of India I used this to advertise the tightest home-loan rate band that still included at least one genuine quote from every lender, so the advertisement was honest for all of them. I kept one live rate per lender in a heap, tracked the running maximum, and remembered the narrowest covering band. Explaining the heap-min-to-running-max invariant, why advancing the minimum is what shrinks the window, and the exhaustion stop condition is what shows an interviewer that I understand this subtle K-way Merge variant.
